Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that shotgun pleadings that fail to give defendants adequate notice of the claims against them should be dismissed.

Cite at least six decisions of the Eleventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.

answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**The District Court Properly Dismissed the Complaint as a Shotgun Pleading That Denied Defendant Adequate Notice.**

A complaint must give the defendant fair notice of each claim and the grounds on which it rests. *Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544, 555 (2007). A shotgun pleading does not. This Court reviews a dismissal on that ground for abuse of discretion, *Vibe Micro, Inc. v. Shabanets*, 878 F.3d 1291, 1294 (11th Cir. 2018), and none occurred here.

**A. This Court has repeatedly condemned shotgun pleadings.**

This Court has identified four general types of shotgun pleadings: (1) a complaint whose multiple counts each adopt the allegations of all preceding counts; (2) a complaint replete with conclusory, vague, and immaterial facts not obviously connected to any particular cause of action; (3) a complaint that does not separate each cause of action or claim for relief into a different count; and (4) a complaint that asserts multiple claims against multiple defendants without specifying which defendant is responsible for which acts or omissions, or which defendant each claim is brought against. *Weiland v. Palm Beach Cnty. Sheriff's Off.*, 792 F.3d 1313, 1321–23 (11th Cir. 2015). "The unifying characteristic of all types of shotgun pleadings is that they fail to one degree or another, and in one way or another, to give the defendants adequate notice of the claims against them and the grounds upon which each claim rests." *Id.* at 1323.

The Court's concern is longstanding. In *Anderson v. District Board of Trustees of Central Florida Community College*, 77 F.3d 364, 366–67 (11th Cir. 1996), the Court criticized a complaint that made it "virtually impossible to know which allegations of fact are intended to support which claim(s) for relief." Counts that sweep in everything pleaded before them force the defendant and the court to sift out what is material to each theory. *See Strategic Income Fund, L.L.C. v. Spear, Leeds & Kellogg Corp.*, 305 F.3d 1293, 1295 (11th Cir. 2002). Lumping defendants together compounds the problem. *Magluta v. Samples*, 256 F.3d 1282, 1284 (11th Cir. 2001) (condemning a "shotgun" complaint that incorporated prior allegations into successive counts and attributed conduct to the defendants collectively).

**B. The Complaint fails to give Defendant adequate notice.**

The Complaint bears the hallmarks this Court has condemned. [Identify the applicable defects with record citations: counts incorporating all preceding allegations; immaterial or conclusory allegations untethered to any count; multiple theories combined in a single count; and collective allegations against multiple defendants.] As a result, Defendant cannot reasonably determine what it is alleged to have done, which facts support each count, or which legal theory it must answer. [Provide a concrete example from a specific count.]

Plaintiff cannot cure that defect by pointing to isolated allegations scattered through the pleading. Neither Defendant nor the court should have to assemble Plaintiff's claims for him. *Weiland* does not require a different result. Although the Court there declined to condemn the relevant counts merely because they reincorporated factual allegations, it did so where the pleading still adequately informed the defendants of the claims and their factual bases. *See* 792 F.3d at 1323–26. The question is notice, and this Complaint does not provide it.

**C. Dismissal was an appropriate exercise of discretion.**

The harm extends beyond Defendant. Shotgun pleadings burden the trial court's docket, broaden and blur discovery, and impose unwarranted expense on litigants and courts. *See Cramer v. Florida*, 117 F.3d 1258, 1263 (11th Cir. 1997). A defendant confronted with such a pleading need not guess at its meaning and answer; it may seek repleading before the case proceeds. *See Wagner v. First Horizon Pharm. Corp.*, 464 F.3d 1273, 1279–80 (11th Cir. 2006); *Anderson*, 77 F.3d at 366–67.

District courts may also dismiss on this basis. *See Vibe Micro*, 878 F.3d at 1294–96 (affirming dismissal of shotgun pleading). A plaintiff should ordinarily receive one chance to remedy the deficiencies before dismissal with prejudice. *See id.* at 1295–96. [Describe the notice of defects and the opportunity to replead that Plaintiff received, and how Plaintiff failed to use it.] Having received that opportunity, Plaintiff has no basis to demand another. The judgment should be affirmed.
